usage: 아침에 세수해요
I wash my face in the morning
아침에 marks the time 'in the morning'; 세수하다 means specifically the face, not the whole body.
세수하고 자요
I wash my face and go to sleep
-고 chains two actions in sequence; a typical bedtime-routine collocation.
비누로 세수해요
I wash my face with soap
비누로 = 'with soap'; the 로 particle marks the tool/means.
세수만 하고 나왔어요
I just washed my face and came out
세수만 = 'only washing the face' (no makeup, etc.); 만 means 'only'.
examples: 일어나서 세수해요
I get up and wash my face
-아서 links 'get up' and 'wash' as one connected flow of waking up.
찬물로 세수했어요
I washed my face with cold water
찬물로 = 'with cold water'; many Koreans say cold water wakes them up.
빨리 세수하고 학교 가야지
Hurry, wash your face and get to school
-아야지 is a soft self-urging/nudging ending a parent uses to a child.
nuance: 세수하다 means specifically to wash your face (얼굴), built from the Sino-Korean noun 세수 (洗手, literally 'wash-hands', an old word that drifted to mean washing the face) plus 하다. Korean splits washing by body part, and this is the English-speaker pitfall: 씻다 is the broad 'wash (hands/body)', 샤워하다 is the whole body under water, and 감다 is reserved for hair — so '머리를 세수하다' or 'I'll wash (=shower) with 세수하다' are both wrong. Because it is a 하다 verb, the everyday form is just 세수해요, and the negative naturally splits the noun off as 세수 안 해요 rather than 안 세수해요. It collocates with 아침에, 찬물로/비누로, and chains with -고 into routines (세수하고 자요).

structuredNuance.t: 세수하다 means specifically to wash your face (얼굴). Korean splits washing by body part, so this verb covers the face only.
씻다 is the broad 'wash (hands/body)', 샤워하다 is the whole body under water, and 감다 is reserved for hair. 세수하다 is the face alone.

mistakes: Don't use 세수하다 for showering — it only covers the face; the whole body is 샤워하다 (or 씻다).
Don't put the negative as 안 세수해요; 하다-verbs split it as 세수 안 해요, which sounds far more natural.

usage: 밥 먹고 양치해요
I brush my teeth after eating
밥 먹고 (= after eating) is the most common trigger phrase for brushing.
하루에 세 번 양치해요
I brush my teeth three times a day
하루에 세 번 = 'three times a day'; 에 marks the frequency-per-unit.
칫솔로 양치해요
I brush my teeth with a toothbrush
칫솔로 = 'with a toothbrush'; 로 marks the tool.
양치 좀 하고 와
Go brush your teeth (and come back)
Casual nudge; 좀 softens it, -고 와 = 'do it and come back'.
examples: 자기 전에 양치해요
I brush my teeth before bed
자기 전에 = 'before sleeping'; -기 전에 attaches to the dictionary stem.
양치하고 학교에 가요
I brush my teeth and go to school
-고 chains the morning routine; 학교에 marks the destination with 에.
양치 안 하면 충치 생겨요
If you don't brush, you'll get cavities
-(으)면 = 'if'; 충치 생기다 = 'a cavity forms', a real-life warning.
nuance: 양치하다 (also 양치질하다) is the natural daily word for brushing your teeth, from the Sino-Korean noun 양치 (養齒, 'care for the teeth') plus 하다. Its near-twin is 이를 닦다, literally 'wipe/scrub the teeth' — the two are interchangeable in most settings, though 이를 닦다 foregrounds the physical scrubbing while 양치(질)하다 names the whole hygiene act (it also covers rinsing the mouth). The English-speaker pitfall is word choice for 'teeth': say 이 or 치아, never 이빨, which is blunt/animal-register and sounds rude about a person's mouth — so 이빨을 닦다 is to be avoided. Like other 하다 routine verbs it splits the negative as 양치 안 해요, and it habitually pairs with 밥 먹고, 자기 전에, and 칫솔로.

mistakes: Don't say 이빨을 닦다 — 이빨 is casual/animal vocabulary; use 양치하다 or 이를 닦다.
Don't form the negative as 안 양치해요; the 하다 verb splits it as 양치 안 해요.

usage: 운동하고 샤워해요
I take a shower after exercising
운동하고 = 'after working out'; -고 chains the two actions.
따뜻한 물로 샤워했어요
I showered with warm water
따뜻한 물로 = 'with warm water'; 로 marks the means.
찬물로 샤워해요
I take a cold shower
찬물로 = 'with cold water'; contrasts with 따뜻한 물로.
샤워부터 할게요
I'll shower first
샤워부터 = 'starting with a shower'; 부터 = 'from/first'.
examples: 매일 아침에 샤워해요
I take a shower every morning
매일 아침에 = 'every morning'; states a daily habit.
지금 샤워하고 싶어요
I want to take a shower now
-고 싶어요 = 'want to'; expresses a present desire.
땀 흘려서 빨리 샤워해야겠어요
I sweated, so I'd better shower soon
-아서 gives the reason; -아야겠다 = 'I'd better', a resolve to act.
nuance: 샤워하다 means to take a shower, made from the English loanword 샤워 (shower) plus 하다 — so it carries no 한자. The key distinction is mode of washing: 샤워하다 is standing under running water, whereas 목욕하다 (沐浴) is soaking in a filled tub, and 씻다 is the generic 'wash up'; English 'take a bath' must NOT be rendered 샤워하다. A second pitfall is that English lets you 'take a shower' (with 'take'), but Korean glues the action into one verb — there is no 샤워를 가지다 / 샤워를 받다; just say 샤워해요. As a 하다 verb the negative splits to 샤워 안 해요, and it collocates with 운동하고, 따뜻한/찬물로, and 매일 아침에.

structuredNuance.t: 샤워하다 means to take a shower — standing under running water.

mistakes: Don't use 샤워하다 for soaking in a bathtub — that's 목욕하다; 샤워하다 is washing under running water.
Don't translate 'take a shower' word-for-word as 샤워를 받다/가지다; Korean just says 샤워해요.

usage: 밥 먹고 설거지해요
I wash the dishes after eating
밥 먹고 = 'after eating'; the most natural cue for dishwashing.
설거지는 제가 할게요
I'll do the dishes
는 topicalizes the chore; -ㄹ게요 = 'I'll' (a volunteering offer).
설거지가 쌓였어요
The dishes have piled up
설거지 here means the dishes-to-wash; 쌓이다 = 'pile up'.
설거지를 도와줄까요?
Shall I help with the dishes?
도와주다 = 'help'; -ㄹ까요? offers help politely.
examples: 저녁 먹고 설거지했어요
I washed the dishes after dinner
저녁 먹고 = 'after dinner'; pairs the chore with a meal.
오늘은 설거지하기 싫어요
I don't feel like doing the dishes today
-기 싫어요 = 'don't feel like doing'; 오늘은 contrasts 'today (at least)'.
설거지는 식기세척기가 다 해요
The dishwasher does all the dishes
식기세척기 = 'dishwasher (machine)'; 다 = 'all', a real-home situation.
nuance: 설거지하다 is the everyday word for washing up the dishes after a meal, from the native (non-Sino) noun 설거지 plus 하다. Unlike 씻다 (wash any single object) or 닦다 (wipe/scrub), 설거지 names the whole post-meal task — gathering, washing, and rinsing all the dishes — so a single cup is normally 컵을 씻다, but the whole sink-load is 설거지(를) 하다. The famous pitfall here is spelling, not meaning: it is 설거지, never 설겆이 or 설겆지 (the old 설겆- form was abolished), and learners constantly misspell it. As a 하다 verb the negative splits to 설거지 안 해요, and the noun itself can stand in for 'the dirty dishes' (설거지가 쌓이다). It is commonly offered politely as 설거지는 제가 할게요.

usage: 이 옷은 손으로 세탁해요
I wash these clothes by hand
손으로 = 'by hand'; 로 marks the method, contrasting with the machine.
주말에 이불을 세탁했어요
I washed the blanket on the weekend
이불 (bedding) shows 세탁하다 also covers big launderable items.
세탁소에 맡겼어요
I dropped it off at the cleaner's
세탁소 = 'laundry/dry-cleaner's'; 맡기다 = 'leave (in someone's care)'.
드라이클리닝으로 세탁하세요
Please dry-clean it
드라이클리닝으로 = 'by dry cleaning'; a care-method instruction.
examples: 흰옷은 따로 세탁해요
I wash white clothes separately
따로 = 'separately'; a basic laundry-sorting rule.
이건 찬물에 세탁하세요
Please wash this in cold water
찬물에 = 'in cold water'; the wording you see on care tags.
이 셔츠는 손세탁만 가능해요
This shirt can only be hand-washed
손세탁 = 'hand wash'; -만 가능하다 = 'only ... is possible', tag language.
nuance: 세탁하다 means to launder or wash clothes, from the Sino-Korean noun 세탁 (洗濯, 'wash-rinse') plus 하다. Its everyday partner is 빨래하다: 빨래(하다) is the casual, spoken 'do the wash' you say at home, while 세탁(하다) sounds a touch more formal/technical and is what appears on washing machines, care labels, and shop signs (세탁소 = the cleaner's; 손세탁 = hand wash; 드라이 = dry clean). The pitfall is keeping the place and the act apart — 세탁소 is the shop (a noun for the location), not the verb, so you don't '세탁소하다'. Note too the body-part split elsewhere: clothes are 세탁/빨래, but hair is 감다 and the body is 씻다. It collocates with 손으로, 찬물에, 따로, and 흰옷은.

mistakes: Don't confuse 세탁소 (the laundry shop) with the act 세탁하다 — the shop is a place noun, the verb is the action.

english: to tidy up / to put in order
usage: 책상을 정돈해요
I tidy up my desk
책상 (desk) is a typical target; 정돈하다 = arrange neatly into place.
신발을 가지런히 정돈했어요
I lined up the shoes neatly
가지런히 = 'neatly, in an even row'; a signature adverb for 정돈.
머리를 단정하게 정돈했어요
I neatened up my hair
정돈하다 also covers tidying one's appearance/hair, not just objects.
정리정돈을 잘해요
I'm good at keeping things tidy
정리정돈 = the set phrase 'sorting and ordering'; very common together.
examples: 방을 깨끗이 정돈해요
I tidy my room nice and clean
깨끗이 = 'cleanly'; describes the orderly end state.
서류를 순서대로 정돈했어요
I put the documents in order
순서대로 = 'in order/sequence'; 정돈 arranges them into sequence.
자기 전에 책상을 정돈해 두세요
Tidy your desk (and leave it that way) before bed
-아 두다 = 'do in advance and leave it'; a gentle instruction.
nuance: 정돈하다 means to put things into neat order — straightening, lining up, and arranging items so they look orderly — from the Sino-Korean 정돈 (整頓, 'arrange-settle') plus 하다. Its constant near-synonym is 정리하다 (整理, 'arrange-manage'), and the dividing line matters: 정돈하다 leans toward making the existing things look tidy and aligned, while 정리하다 leans toward sorting out, deciding what to keep, and clearing away the excess — so '필요 없는 물건을 정돈하다' is odd; throwing things out is 정리하다. The two so often co-occur that they fuse into the fixed phrase 정리정돈. The pitfall for English speakers is treating 'tidy up' as one word: don't reach for 정돈 when you mean 'clean (remove dirt)' — that is 청소하다. It collocates with 가지런히, 깨끗이, 책상을, and 단정하게.

mistakes: 정돈하다 is arranging neatly, not discarding — to clear out or sort what to keep, use 정리하다.
Don't use 정돈하다 for cleaning off dirt/dust; that's 청소하다 (정돈 is about order, not grime).

usage: 방을 예쁘게 꾸며요
I decorate my room prettily
예쁘게 = 'prettily'; 을/를 marks the space being decorated.
오늘 예쁘게 꾸몄네요
You dressed up nicely today
꾸미다 also = dressing yourself up; -네요 adds friendly notice.
화장으로 얼굴을 꾸며요
I do up my face with makeup
화장으로 = 'with makeup'; 로 marks the means of decorating.
이야기를 꾸며 냈어요
He made up a story
꾸며 내다 = 'fabricate/invent'; a second sense of 꾸미다 = 'concoct'.
examples: 크리스마스에 집을 꾸며요
I decorate the house at Christmas
에 marks the occasion; decorating a place for an event.
언니가 방을 예쁘게 꾸몄어요
My (older) sister decorated her room prettily
꾸몄어요 (꾸미+었) is the past, describing the finished result.
데이트 가는데 좀 꾸미고 싶어요
I'm going on a date, so I want to dress up a bit
-는데 sets the background; 좀 softens '(dress up) a little'.
nuance: 꾸미다 is a native verb covering a spread of 'make (something) look a certain way': decorate a space (방을 꾸미다), doll yourself up (예쁘게 꾸미다), and even fabricate/concoct (이야기를 꾸미다, 음모를 꾸미다 = 'hatch a plot'). The nearest neighbor is 장식하다 (裝飾, 'decorate'), which is narrower and more formal — it fits ornaments and displays (트리를 장식하다) but cannot mean 'dress oneself up', where only 꾸미다 works. Grammatically it is a regular ㅣ-stem verb, so 꾸미 + 어 contracts to 꾸며 → 꾸며요, past 꾸몄어요 (never 꾸미어요). The decorated thing takes 을/를 and an adverb like 예쁘게 or 멋있게 usually rides along. The pitfall: don't over-apply the English 'decorate'; you 꾸미다 a person, but a cake/dish is more often 장식하다.

usage: 머리를 감아요
I wash my hair
머리를 is the fixed object; 감다 is the dedicated verb for hair.
매일 머리를 감아요
I wash my hair every day
매일 = 'every day'; states a routine frequency.
샴푸로 머리를 감아요
I wash my hair with shampoo
샴푸로 = 'with shampoo'; 로 marks the means.
머리 감을 시간이 없어요
I don't have time to wash my hair
감을 (future adnominal) + 시간 = 'time to wash'; -ㄹ 시간이 없다.
examples: 아침에 머리를 감았어요
I washed my hair in the morning
감았어요 (감+았) is the past; a daily-routine statement.
머리 감고 말려요
I wash my hair and dry it
-고 chains it with 말리다 (to dry); the natural next step.
오늘은 귀찮아서 머리 안 감았어요
I was too lazy today, so I didn't wash my hair
-아서 gives the reason; a very real-life confession.
nuance: 감다 is the body-part-specific verb for washing hair, and it almost always takes 머리 as its object (머리를 감다) — this part-by-part split is the core pitfall for English speakers, whose one verb 'wash' tempts them into 머리를 씻다, which Koreans don't say. Reserve 씻다 for hands/body, 세수하다 for the face, and 감다 for hair. Grammatically it is a regular consonant-stem verb, so 감 + 아요 → 감아요, past 감았어요, and the honorific request adds the linking 으: 감으세요. One trap to file away: an identical-looking homonym 감다 also means 'to close (the eyes)' (눈을 감다) and another 'to wind/wrap', so only context and the object (머리 vs 눈) tell them apart. It chains naturally as 머리를 감고 말리다.

It is a regular consonant-stem verb, so 감 + 아요 → 감아요, past 감았어요, and the honorific request adds the linking 으: 감으세요.

Also file away an identical-looking homonym 감다 meaning 'to close (the eyes)' (눈을 감다) and another 'to wind/wrap', so only context and the object (머리 vs 눈) tell them apart.

mistakes: Don't say 머리를 씻다 — hair takes 감다, not 씻다; 씻다 is for hands/body.
Don't drop the linking vowel in commands: it's 감으세요 (consonant stem + 으세요), not 감세요.

usage: 머리를 말려요
I dry my hair
머리를 = object; 말리다 is transitive 'make (it) dry'.
빨래를 밖에서 말려요
I dry the laundry outside
밖에서 = 'outside (at)'; 에서 marks where the drying happens.
드라이기로 머리를 말려요
I dry my hair with a hair dryer
드라이기로 = 'with a hair dryer'; 로 marks the tool.
젖은 옷을 말려야 해요
I need to dry the wet clothes
젖은 = 'wet (that got wet)'; -아야 해요 = 'have to'.
examples: 수건을 햇빛에 말려요
I dry the towel in the sunlight
햇빛에 = 'in the sunlight'; 에 marks the location/medium.
머리를 안 말리고 자면 감기 걸려요
If you sleep without drying your hair, you'll catch a cold
-고 자다 = 'sleep without doing'; a classic Korean caution.
장마철엔 빨래가 잘 안 말라요
In the rainy season the laundry doesn't dry well
Here 마르다 (intransitive 'dry up') is used — note the contrast with 말리다.
nuance: 말리다 means to dry something out — hair, laundry, wet shoes — and it is transitive, so it takes 을/를 for the thing you dry. Crucially distinguish it from its intransitive partner 마르다 ('become dry' by itself): YOU 빨래를 말리다 (you dry the laundry), but the laundry 빨래가 마르다 (the laundry dries) — picking the wrong one is the top pitfall, since English 'dry' is both. Grammatically 말리다 is a regular ㅣ-stem verb: 말리 + 어 → 말려요, past 말렸어요 (never 말리어요). Beware a same-spelled homonym 말리다 meaning 'to stop / talk someone out of' (싸움을 말리다), so context decides; anchor the 'dry' sense first. It pairs with 드라이기로, 햇빛에, 밖에서, and chains after 감다 (머리 감고 말려요).

english: to apply / to put on (cream, etc.)
usage: 로션을 발라요
I put on lotion
로션을 = object; 바르다 = spread/apply onto skin or a surface.
선크림을 꼭 바르세요
Be sure to put on sunscreen
꼭 = 'be sure to, definitely'; a strong recommendation.
얼굴에 크림을 발라요
I put cream on my face
얼굴에 = 'onto the face'; 에 marks the surface receiving it.
입술에 립밤을 발랐어요
I put lip balm on my lips
입술에 = 'on the lips'; shows the 에(surface)+을(stuff) pattern.
examples: 세수하고 로션을 발라요
I wash my face and put on lotion
-고 chains the steps; a basic morning skincare order.
빵에 잼을 발랐어요
I spread jam on the bread
빵에 = 'onto the bread'; 바르다 also covers spreading food.
상처에 연고를 골고루 발라 주세요
Please spread the ointment evenly on the wound
골고루 = 'evenly'; -아 주세요 makes it a polite request to apply it.
nuance: 바르다 means to apply or spread a thin layer of something onto a surface — lotion, sunscreen, jam, ointment. The two-part frame is the thing applied + 을/를 and the surface + 에 (얼굴에 로션을 발라요), and getting that 에 right is a frequent pitfall: English 'put on my face' tempts 얼굴을 바르다, but the face is the surface (에), not the object. Distinguish it from neighbors: 칠하다 is to paint/coat a broad surface (벽을 칠하다 = paint a wall), and 묻히다 is to get/dab a substance onto something more loosely — 바르다 implies deliberate, spread-out application. Conjugation is the headline grammar point: 바르다 is 르-irregular, so before -아/어 the 르 drops and an extra ㄹ appears, giving 발라요 and past 발랐어요 — never 바르어요/바르었어요.

mistakes: Because it's 르-irregular, the past is 발랐어요, not 바르었어요 (and present 발라요, not 바르어요).
Don't mark the surface with 을/를 — it's 얼굴에 크림을 바르다 (surface takes 에), not 얼굴을 바르다.

usage: 머리를 빗어요
I comb my hair
머리를 = object; 빗다 = comb/run a comb through the hair.
빗으로 머리를 빗어요
I comb my hair with a comb
빗으로 = 'with a comb'; note the noun 빗 (comb) inside the verb 빗다.
머리를 곱게 빗어요
I comb my hair smooth and neat
곱게 = 'prettily/smoothly'; a typical adverb for grooming.
머리 좀 빗고 나가
Comb your hair before you go out
-고 나가다 = 'do, then go out'; 좀 softens the nudge.
examples: 아침에 머리를 빗어요
I comb my hair in the morning
아침에 = 'in the morning'; part of getting ready.
머리를 단정하게 빗었어요
I combed my hair neatly
단정하게 = 'neatly, tidily'; 빗었어요 (빗+었) is the past.
엉킨 머리를 살살 빗으세요
Please comb the tangled hair gently
엉킨 = 'tangled'; 살살 = 'gently', a careful instruction.
nuance: 빗다 means to comb or brush through your hair, taking 머리 as its object; the tool is the noun 빗 (a comb), so 빗으로 머리를 빗다 literally stacks 'comb with a comb'. Note the distinction from 빗기다 — the causative/transitive 'comb someone else's hair' (아이 머리를 빗기다), used when a parent grooms a child. Grammatically it is a regular consonant-stem verb: 빗 + 어요 → 빗어요, past 빗었어요, with the linking 으 in commands (빗으세요). The pitfall is its lookalikes: don't confuse 빗다 (comb) with 씻다 (wash) or the homophone-in-some-forms 빛(light)/빚(debt) — they sound close but are entirely different. It collocates with 단정하게, 곱게, 빗으로, and 아침에.

To comb SOMEONE ELSE'S hair (e.g. a child's), use the causative 빗기다, not plain 빗다.

usage: 아침에 동생을 깨워요
I wake my younger sibling in the morning
동생을 = object; 깨우다 takes the person being woken.
일곱 시에 깨워 주세요
Please wake me at seven
-아 주세요 = 'please do (for me)'; handy at a hotel/guesthouse.
알람으로 깨워요
I wake (him) up with an alarm
알람으로 = 'with an alarm'; 로 marks the means.
자는 사람을 깨우지 마세요
Don't wake a sleeping person
자는 사람 = 'a person who is sleeping'; -지 마세요 = 'please don't'.
examples: 엄마가 저를 깨웠어요
My mom woke me up
깨웠어요 (깨우+었→깨웠) is the past; someone waking you.
아이를 깨우지 마세요
Please don't wake the child
-지 마세요 = polite prohibition; let the child sleep.
내일 일찍 깨워 줄 수 있어요?
Can you wake me early tomorrow?
일찍 = 'early'; -아 줄 수 있어요? politely asks a favor.
nuance: 깨우다 is the transitive 'wake someone up', so it always takes a person as its object (저를 깨워요) — this is the pitfall, because English 'wake up' is both transitive and intransitive. 깨우다 is the causative of 깨다 ('wake up by oneself', as in 잠에서 깨다), and it contrasts with 일어나다 ('get up, rise from bed'): to say YOU woke and got out of bed, use 일어나다/깨다, and reserve 깨우다 for rousing another person. Conjugation: the stem ends in 우, so 우 + 어 contracts to 워, giving 깨워요 and past 깨웠어요. The set request 깨워 주세요 ('please wake me') is one of the most useful travel phrases. It collocates with 아침에, 일찍, 알람으로, and the person-object + 을/를.

mistakes: Use 깨우다 to wake SOMEONE ELSE; to say you yourself wake/get up, use 일어나다 or 깨다.
The contracted form is 깨워요 (깨우 + 어 → 깨워), not 깨우어요.

usage: 그릇을 물로 헹궈요
I rinse the dish with water
물로 = 'with water'; 헹구다 = rinse off with clean water.
입을 헹구세요
Please rinse your mouth
입을 헹구다 = 'rinse the mouth'; heard at the dentist or after brushing.
깨끗한 물에 헹궈요
I rinse it in clean water
깨끗한 물에 = 'in clean water'; 에 marks the rinsing medium.
한 번 더 헹궈 주세요
Please rinse it one more time
한 번 더 = 'one more time'; -아 주세요 requests the extra rinse.
examples: 설거지하고 깨끗이 헹궈요
I wash the dishes and rinse them clean
-고 chains it after 설거지하다; the natural finishing step.
채소를 흐르는 물에 헹궜어요
I rinsed the vegetables under running water
흐르는 물에 = 'under running water'; 헹궜어요 (헹구+었) is the past.
샴푸를 충분히 헹궈야 머릿결이 좋아져요
You have to rinse out the shampoo well for healthy hair
충분히 = 'thoroughly'; -아야 = 'only if you ...', a real hair-care tip.
nuance: 헹구다 means to rinse something with clean water to flush off soap, dirt, or residue — dishes, vegetables, laundry, or your mouth. It is the final clean-water step that follows the actual washing, which is exactly its dividing line from 씻다: 씻다 is the broad 'wash (with soap/scrubbing)', while 헹구다 specifically removes what's left using plain water, so '비누로 헹구다' is odd — you 씻다 with soap, then 헹구다 with water. The object takes 을/를 and the water takes 에/로 (흐르는 물에 헹구다). Conjugation: the stem ends in 우, so 우 + 어 contracts to 궈, giving 헹궈요 and past 헹궜어요 — a common misspelling is 헹구어요/헹궈어요, both wrong. It chains after 설거지하다 and 씻다 and pairs with 흐르는 물에, 깨끗이, 충분히.
